Adult Alaska pollock in the Bering Sea can attain a maximum total length of 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], a size that places them among the larger gadids in the North Pacific. Females that reach this ultimate size are estimated to have an ultimate wet weight of approximately 5,400 grams [Wwi = approximately 5,400 grams], a value derived from length-weight regressions for the species. This substantial body mass supports a life history characterized by high fecundity, as the species is a batch spawner capable of producing numerous clutches annually. Field studies have documented that females release approximately 1,100 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,100 eggs per spawning event], and under favorable conditions, they can produce over 100 such batches within a single reproductive season [F_R_i = 100 such batches within a single reproductive season]. This extraordinarily high reproductive output is sustained only when water temperatures remain near 6 °C [T = 6 °C], as cooler conditions dramatically reduce spawning frequency and egg viability.

The transition from a pelagic larva to a demersal juvenile marks a critical period in the life cycle of Gadus chalcogrammus. Newly hatched individuals, which emerge from small, yolk-laden eggs, weigh only about 0.0008 grams [Wwb = about 0.0008 grams] at birth. This low birth mass reflects the high fecundity and small egg size typical of batch-spawning gadids, where energetic investment per offspring is minimized to maximize offspring number. The onset of exogenous feeding occurs rapidly as the yolk-sac larva develops functional jaws and a differentiated retina, typically within a few days after hatching. The incubation period from fertilization to hatching, during which the embryo relies entirely on its yolk reserves, has been estimated at approximately 9 days [ab = approximately 9 days] when eggs are maintained at a stable temperature of 9.4 °C [T = 9.4 °C]. Warmer incubation temperatures can shorten this period, while cooler ones prolong it, illustrating the strong thermal sensitivity of early developmental processes in this species.

Sexual maturation in Alaska pollock is attained at a relatively small body size compared to the species' maximum. Puberty, defined as the onset of gonad development and the first commitment to gametogenesis, occurs when females reach a total length of 36.9 centimeters [Lp = 36.9 centimeters]. The corresponding wet weight at this size, estimated from the same length-weight relationship used for adults, is 357 grams [Wwp = 357 grams]. This represents a substantial investment in somatic growth before the initiation of reproductive activity, a pattern common among iteroparous gadids that inhabit highly seasonal environments. The shift from somatic to reproductive allocation is accompanied by an activation of the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, which drives vitellogenesis in females and spermiation in males. Once mature, individuals typically spawn for the first time in their third or fourth year, although this schedule can vary with local productivity regimes and thermal conditions.

The maximum longevity of Alaska pollock is a key parameter for understanding population turnover and resilience to fishing pressure. Field records indicate that the longest-lived individuals in the Bering Sea reach an age of approximately 28 years [am = approximately 28 years], a lifespan that is relatively extended for a gadid of this size and at a temperature of 6 °C [T = 6 °C]metabolic rate. This maximum lifespan has been observed in populations inhabiting the cooler, deeper portions of the continental shelf where water temperatures average around 6 °C [T = 6 °C], conditions that likely slow the rate of physiological aging and senescence. At such advanced ages, females may exceed 60 centimeters in length and produce more than 150,000 eggs per batch, though their somatic condition often declines as reproductive senescence progresses. The species' longevity is also reflected in its high survival rates during the adult stage, which compensate for the extremely high mortality experienced during the early larval and juvenile phases.

Comparative studies across the genus Gadus reveal considerable variation in life-history traits, with Alaska pollock occupying an intermediate position between the faster-growing Atlantic cod and the slower-growing Greenland cod. Within the genus Gadus, Alaska pollock reaches an ultimate total length of 91 centimeters [Li = 91 centimeters], smaller than the maximum sizes reported for Gadus morhua exceeding 150 centimeters, yet larger than the typical maxima for Arctic gadids. Under optimal thermal conditions of 6 °C [T = 6 °C], females release approximately 1,100 eggs per spawning event [N_R_i = approximately 1,100 eggs per spawning event] and produce approximately 364 batches per year [F_R_i = approximately 364 batches per year], yielding an annual fecundity of approximately 400,000 eggs per female — a high output necessary given the low survival probabilities faced by the minute, 0.0008 gram [Wwb = 0.0008 gram] hatchlings as they transition from the yolk-sac stage to active planktonic feeding. The minute hatchling mass places Alaska pollock among the gadids with the smallest neonates, a trait linked to their exceptionally high fecundity and low per-offspring investment.
